This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronan.
Brazil's leftist president Lula da Silva
has been reelected to his fourth term.
Lula fended off a challenge from Flavio Bolsonaro,
the son of the country's former president
who is now in prison after being convicted
on corruption charges after he left office.
This was a runoff election after neither candidate
received 50% in the first round of voting.
Tonight, Lula received nearly 52%
compared to Bolsonaro's more than 48.
Lula's victory is a setback to Bolsonaro
and his effort to return the presidency to his family.
Bolsonaro also had the support of President Trump
and said he wanted to have closer ties to the U.S.
For the 80-year-old Lula,
this is his fourth non-consecutive term in office.
It's the first time a candidate in Brazil has lost
in the first round of voting and come back to win.
The competitive landscape for this year's midterm election
is stretching deep into places
that voted for President Trump in 2024.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reports that includes Arkansas.
In the last month, both parties have spent millions of dollars
in Arkansas, and Republicans have quintupled their ad spend
in the state's second congressional district,
according to Ad Impact data.
Democratic nominee Chris Jones says it's because
they know affordability concerns
have people looking for change.
-Folks are literally hurting,
and it's to the point where they're saying,
"My life is so bad that I don't care about party anymore.
Like, I'll look past party
in order to change my conditions right now."
-The Senate contest between incumbent Republican Tom Cotton
and Democrat Hallie Schaffner has flown under the radar
compared to many other red-state races
that have become competitive,
but Republicans have spent big there, too,
to try and maintain that seat.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News, Little Rock, Arkansas.
-Israel will hold a national election Tuesday
with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
facing his former military chief of staff, Gotti Eisenkot,
who's promising more diplomacy and less military action.
In the Four Corners region,
flooding has impacted some 2,000 people
in Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah,
from member station KUM Ann and Albuquerque.
Meghan Kamrick reports.
-San Juan County officials say waters are receding
and rescue operations are mostly complete,
but they are warning residents
to not enter evacuated areas or homes.
-County undersheriff Corey Tanner says hidden hazards
include raw sewage and chemicals in the water,
as well as damaged utility infrastructure.
He urges residents to be patient,
so authorities can go house by house to check for hazards.
-As far as we know, we've got through this
without any significant injury or deaths.
God help us. We don't want that to be someone walking
into a house and flipping on a light switch with a gas leak.
-New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham
is seeking a federal emergency disaster declaration.
Another round of storms could hit the region later this week.
For NPR News, I'm Meghan Kamrick in Albuquerque.
-It's NPR.
Two Midwestern Catholic bishops released statements Sunday,
expressing regret about Thursday's White House
meeting with President Trump after a photo was released
with them praying with the president.
Milwaukee archbishop Jeffrey Grove offered a public apology
and said he felt manipulated by the meeting.
-The Bishop of Des Moines, Iowa, William Johnson,
issued a similar statement saying the White House
took advantage of the religious leaders
by publishing the -- distributing the picture
that they said should not have been released
because it appeared they were engaging in politics.
Hollywood had another strong weekend in theaters.
NPR's Bob Mundello says the top films
have something in common.
-When it comes to this week's box office leaders,
there will be blood, as it were.
-In "Clayface," a DC Comics adaptation that took the top spot,
the lead character's blood is filled with nanotech agents
that cause him to change shape.
-What's happening to me?
-In "You Can See Everything,"
Nathan Fielder's runner-up at the box office,
it's convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes
and her blood testing scam that are central.
-You really feel you did nothing wrong?
-I did not.
-An infusion of 1,800 new screens
helped "You Can See Everything" come close in its second weekend
to topping the opening of the well-reviewed supervillain movie.
The almost three-hour documentary remains
in fewer theaters than "Clayface,"
but it played to more patrons per theater.
Bob Mundello, NPR News.
-Six Flags says it will install secondary seatbelts
on its roller coaster at the Atlanta amusement park
after a man died two weeks ago when he was thrown from the ride.
I'm Dan Ronan, NPR News.
-Support for NPR -- -This message comes
from Cure Alzheimer's Fund.
From family to community, connections
and the memories they make are everything.

topics.text: Brazil's Lula da Silva reelected to fourth term, defeating Flavio Bolsonaro in runoff
Arkansas midterm races draw heavy ad spending from both parties, including Senate race between Cotton and Schaffner
Israel to hold national election Tuesday, Netanyahu faces challenger Gotti Eisenkot
Flooding affects about 2,000 people in Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah; New Mexico seeks federal disaster declaration
Two Midwestern Catholic bishops express regret over White House meeting and prayer photo with Trump
Weekend box office led by DC's Clayface, with Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes documentary close behind
Six Flags to add secondary seatbelts on Atlanta coaster after rider died in ejection
